lessons.title: Permanent and induced magnetism, magnetic forces and fields
lessons.summary: Learn how magnetic poles interact, the difference between permanent and induced magnets, how to draw and interpret magnetic fields, why a compass points north, and how an electric current produces a magnetic field that can be used to make an electromagnet.
objectives: I can describe the forces between magnetic poles and explain why magnetism is a non-contact force.
I can explain the difference between permanent and induced magnets.
I can describe a magnetic field, draw field lines for a bar magnet and use a compass to plot them.
I can explain how a compass works and what it tells us about the Earth's core.
I can describe the magnetic field around a current-carrying wire and a solenoid, and explain how an electromagnet works.

activities.title: Magnets and poles
activities.content:
## Poles

Every magnet has two **poles**, a **north-seeking (N) pole** and a **south-seeking (S) pole**, where the magnetic forces are **strongest**. Cut a magnet in half and you get two smaller magnets, each with its own N and S; you can never isolate a single pole.

### Forces between poles
Bring two magnets together and they exert a force on each other:
- **Like poles repel** (N–N or S–S push apart).
- **Unlike poles attract** (N–S pull together).

The force acts even when the magnets are not touching, so magnetism is a **non-contact force**. The force gets weaker as the distance between the magnets increases.

### Magnetic materials
Only a few materials are attracted to magnets. The main **magnetic materials** are **iron, steel, cobalt and nickel**. Copper, aluminium, plastic, wood and most other materials are not magnetic at all.

A magnet **always attracts** an unmagnetised piece of magnetic material; it never repels it. This gives the classic test: **repulsion is the only sure way to prove something is a magnet**, because attraction happens with both magnets and plain lumps of iron.

question.text: A student has two metal bars. One is a magnet and one is an unmagnetised iron bar, but they look identical. What is the only observation that proves a bar is a magnet?
question.hint: A magnet attracts both other magnets and plain iron. What can only a magnet do?
question.explanation: Only two magnets can repel each other. Attraction happens between a magnet and iron too, so attraction proves nothing about which bar is the magnet.

options.text: The bar repels one end of a known magnet
The bar attracts one end of a known magnet
options.feedback: An iron bar would also be attracted.

options.text: The bar attracts a paper clip
options.feedback: The iron bar could be temporarily magnetised by a nearby magnet and do this.

options.text: The bar feels heavier

activities.title: Permanent and induced magnets
activities.content:
## Two kinds of magnet

A **permanent magnet** produces its **own magnetic field** all the time. A fridge magnet or a bar magnet in the lab is a permanent magnet. They are usually made of **steel** or special alloys that keep their magnetism.

An **induced magnet** is a material that **becomes a magnet only when it is placed in a magnetic field**. Hang a chain of paper clips from a bar magnet and each clip becomes an induced magnet that holds the next one. Take the bar magnet away and the clips **quickly lose most or all of their magnetism** and fall apart.

| | Permanent magnet | Induced magnet |
|---|---|---|
| Has its own field? | yes, always | only while in another field |
| Typical material | steel (hard magnetic material) | soft iron |
| Can it repel? | yes | no, induced magnetism always causes **attraction** |

### Why induced magnetism always attracts
When a piece of iron is placed near the N pole of a magnet, the end of the iron closest to the magnet becomes an induced **S** pole. Unlike poles attract, so the iron is pulled towards the magnet. Flip the magnet round and the induced poles flip too, so it is still attracted. That is why a magnet picks up nails regardless of which end you use.

**Soft iron** is used for induced magnets and electromagnet cores because it magnetises and demagnetises easily. **Steel** is used for permanent magnets because it keeps its magnetism.

question.text: True or false: an induced magnet can repel a permanent magnet.
question.hint: Think about which pole is induced nearest to the permanent magnet.
question.explanation: False. The pole induced nearest to the permanent magnet is always the opposite pole, so induced magnetism always results in attraction.

options.text: True
False

activities.title: Magnetic fields
activities.content:
## What is a magnetic field?

A **magnetic field** is the **region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material**. You cannot see it, but you can map it.

### Field lines
We draw a magnetic field using **field lines** with these rules:
- The **direction** of the field at any point is the direction of the force that would act on a **north pole** placed there. So field lines run **from the N pole to the S pole** outside the magnet.
- Lines **never cross**.
- The **closer together** the lines, the **stronger** the field. Lines are most crowded at the **poles**, so the field is strongest there and gets weaker further away.

```
        ╭──────────────────╮
      ╭─┤   N  ▶▶▶▶▶▶  S   ├─╮
      │ ╰──────────────────╯ │
      ╰──────── ◀◀◀ ─────────╯   (lines loop from N round to S)
```

### Plotting a field with a compass
A **plotting compass** is a tiny bar magnet on a pivot. Its needle lines up with the field, with its N end pointing along the field direction.
1. Put the magnet on paper and place the compass near one pole.
2. Mark a dot where the needle's N end points.
3. Move the compass so its tail sits on that dot and repeat.
4. Join the dots to draw one field line, then start again from a different point.

Iron filings sprinkled around a magnet also show the pattern, though not the direction.

### Uniform field
Between two flat, opposite poles held close together the field lines are **parallel and evenly spaced**: a **uniform field** of the same strength everywhere.

question.text: Which THREE statements about magnetic field lines are correct?
question.hint: Think about direction, spacing and where the field is strongest.
question.explanation: Field lines run from N to S outside the magnet, are closest together where the field is strongest (the poles) and never cross. The field is weaker, not stronger, far from the magnet.

options.text: Outside the magnet, field lines point from the north pole to the south pole
Field lines are closest together where the field is strongest
Field lines never cross each other
The field is strongest far away from the magnet
options.feedback: The field is strongest at the poles and weakens with distance.

activities.title: The Earth's magnetic field
activities.content:
## Why does a compass point north?

A compass needle is a small permanent magnet. Left to swing freely it settles pointing roughly **geographic north**. A magnet only lines up like this if it is inside a magnetic field, so this is evidence that **the Earth itself has a magnetic field**.

The field is thought to be produced by movements of the molten iron and nickel in the Earth's **core**. The Earth behaves as if it has a giant bar magnet inside it.

### A slightly confusing fact
The end of a compass needle that points north is its **north-seeking pole**. Unlike poles attract, so the end of the Earth's field near geographic north must actually be a magnetic **south** pole. That is why the poles are more carefully called *north-seeking* and *south-seeking*.

### Uses
- **Navigation**: compasses have guided ships and hikers for centuries.
- **Animals**: some birds and turtles appear to use the Earth's field to migrate.
- **Protection**: the field deflects charged particles from the Sun, which would otherwise strip away the atmosphere. The particles that do get in cause the aurora near the poles.

activities.title: Electromagnetism
activities.content:
## A current makes a magnetic field

When an **electric current flows through a wire, a magnetic field is produced around the wire**. Plotting compasses placed around a vertical wire show the field lines are **concentric circles** centred on the wire.

- The **strength** of the field depends on the **size of the current** (bigger current, stronger field) and the **distance from the wire** (further away, weaker field).
- The **direction** of the field depends on the **direction of the current**. Reverse the current and the field reverses.

**Right-hand grip rule**: point your right thumb along the direction of the (conventional) current and your curled fingers show the direction of the field lines.

## Solenoids
A **solenoid** is a coil of wire. Winding the wire into a coil makes the fields from each turn add up:
- **Inside** the solenoid the field is **strong and uniform** (parallel, evenly spaced lines).
- **Outside**, the field looks exactly like that of a **bar magnet**, with a N pole at one end and a S pole at the other.

### Making it stronger
The field of a solenoid can be increased by:
1. **increasing the current**,
2. **adding more turns** of wire (or packing them closer),
3. putting an **iron core** inside the coil. The iron becomes an induced magnet and greatly increases the field.

A solenoid with an iron core is an **electromagnet**. Unlike a permanent magnet it can be **switched on and off**, its **strength can be varied** by changing the current, and its **poles can be reversed** by reversing the current. Electromagnets are used in scrapyard cranes, electric bells, relays, circuit breakers, door locks and MRI scanners.

question.text: Match each change to an electromagnet with its effect on the magnetic field.
question.hint: Current, turns and core all affect strength; current direction affects the poles.
question.explanation: More current or an iron core makes the field stronger. Reversing the current swaps the N and S poles but does not change the strength.

pairs.left: Reversing the direction of the current

question.text: A long straight wire carries a current vertically upwards. Viewed from above, in which direction do the magnetic field lines go around the wire?
question.hint: Point your right thumb upwards (towards you when viewed from above) and look at the way your fingers curl.
question.explanation: With the thumb of the right hand pointing up (towards the viewer), the fingers curl anticlockwise. So the field lines are anticlockwise circles when seen from above.

options.text: Anticlockwise circles centred on the wire
Clockwise circles centred on the wire
options.feedback: That would be the pattern for a current flowing downwards.

options.text: Straight lines pointing away from the wire
Straight lines parallel to the wire

activities.title: Worked example: designing a scrapyard electromagnet
activities.content:
**A scrapyard crane uses an electromagnet to lift cars. Explain the design choices.**

**Why an electromagnet rather than a permanent magnet?**
The crane needs to pick a car up *and put it down again*. An electromagnet can be **switched off** to release the load; a permanent magnet could not let go.

**Why a soft iron core?**
Soft iron becomes a very strong induced magnet when the current flows, multiplying the field of the coil many times. It also **loses its magnetism as soon as the current stops**, so the car drops cleanly. A steel core would stay magnetised and cling on.

**How can the operator lift a heavier load?**
Increase the **current** through the coil. (Adding more turns would also work but is fixed once the magnet is built.)

**What limits the current?**
The wire heats up as current flows (energy transferred to thermal stores), so there is a maximum safe current for the coil.

**Could the crane lift an aluminium engine block?**
No. Aluminium is not a magnetic material, so the electromagnet exerts no force on it regardless of the current.

question.text: An electric bell uses an electromagnet with a soft iron core rather than a steel core. Explain why soft iron is the better choice.
question.hint: The bell's hammer must move back and forth many times a second, so the magnet has to switch off quickly.
question.explanation: Soft iron is easily magnetised when the current flows, giving a strong field, and it loses its magnetism straight away when the current stops. Steel would remain magnetised and the hammer would stay stuck to the core.

markScheme.criterion: Soft iron is easily magnetised / gives a strong field when current flows
Soft iron loses its magnetism when the current is switched off, whereas steel stays magnetised

question.text:
A student investigates the magnetic field around a bar magnet using a plotting compass.

(a) Describe how the student could use the plotting compass to draw a magnetic field line. (2 marks)

(b) State the direction of the field lines outside the magnet and explain how the student's diagram would show where the field is strongest. (2 marks)

(c) The student then places a piece of unmagnetised iron near the north pole of the magnet. Explain why the iron is attracted. (1 mark)
question.hint: For (a), the compass needle points along the field; mark where it points, then move the compass to that mark.
question.explanation: (a) Place the compass near a pole, mark a dot at the tip of the needle, move the compass so its tail is on the dot, repeat, then join the dots. (b) Lines go from N to S; where they are closest together (at the poles) the field is strongest. (c) The iron becomes an induced magnet with a S pole nearest the magnet's N pole, so unlike poles attract.

markScheme.criterion: Place the compass next to the magnet and mark the position of the needle tip
Move the compass to the mark and repeat, then join the dots
Field lines run from north to south
Field is strongest where the lines are closest together / at the poles
Iron becomes an induced magnet with an opposite pole nearest, so it is attracted

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- Magnets have **N and S poles**; **like poles repel, unlike poles attract**. Magnetism is a **non-contact** force. Only **repulsion** proves something is a magnet.
- Magnetic materials: **iron, steel, cobalt, nickel**.
- **Permanent magnets** (steel) have their own field. **Induced magnets** (soft iron) are magnetic only inside another field and always cause **attraction**.
- A **magnetic field** is the region where a magnetic material feels a force. Field lines go **N → S**, never cross, and are **closest where the field is strongest** (the poles).
- A **compass** is a small magnet that lines up with the field; its behaviour shows the **Earth's core** produces a magnetic field.
- A **current** produces a circular field round a wire (right-hand grip rule). A **solenoid** has a strong uniform field inside and a bar-magnet field outside. Add an **iron core** to make an **electromagnet**; increase current or turns to strengthen it.

practiceQuestions.text: Which THREE of these materials are magnetic?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Iron, nickel and cobalt (and steel, which is mostly iron) are magnetic. Copper and aluminium are not.

options.text: Iron
Nickel
Cobalt
Copper
Aluminium

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: two north poles brought together will attract each other.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Like poles repel; only unlike poles attract.

options.text: True
False

metadata.blanksText: A ___ magnet produces its own magnetic field all the time. An ___ magnet only becomes magnetic when it is placed in a magnetic field.

practiceQuestions.hint: One lasts; the other is caused by something else.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Permanent magnets have their own field; induced magnets are magnetised by another field.

practiceQuestions.text: Where is the magnetic field of a bar magnet strongest?
practiceQuestions.hint: Where are the field lines most crowded?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The field lines are closest together at the poles, so the field is strongest there.

options.text: At the poles
At the centre of the magnet
Halfway between the poles, outside the magnet
It is the same strength everywhere

practiceQuestions.text: Put the steps for plotting a magnetic field line with a plotting compass in the correct order.
practiceQuestions.hint: You must mark where the needle points before moving the compass.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Place the compass near the pole, mark the needle tip, move the compass to the mark, repeat, join the dots.
order: Place the plotting compass close to one pole of the magnet
Mark a dot on the paper at the tip of the compass needle
Move the compass so that the tail of the needle is on the dot
Repeat until you reach the other pole
Join the dots with a smooth line and add an arrow from N to S

practiceQuestions.text: Explain what the behaviour of a compass needle tells us about the Earth.
practiceQuestions.hint: A compass needle only lines up if there is a field for it to line up with.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The needle is a small magnet that always settles pointing north. A magnet only does this inside a magnetic field, so the Earth must have its own magnetic field, produced by its core.

markScheme.criterion: The compass needle is a magnet that lines up pointing north
So the Earth must have a magnetic field / core is magnetic

practiceQuestions.text: What shape are the magnetic field lines around a long straight wire carrying a current?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think of what plotting compasses show when placed around a vertical wire.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The field lines are concentric circles centred on the wire, in a plane at right angles to it.

options.text: Concentric circles centred on the wire
Straight lines parallel to the wire
Straight lines pointing away from the wire
The same as a bar magnet
options.feedback: That is the pattern outside a solenoid, not a straight wire.

practiceQuestions.text: Which THREE changes would increase the strength of an electromagnet?
practiceQuestions.explanation: More current, more turns and an iron core all strengthen the field. Reversing the current only changes the pole directions, and a plastic core does nothing.

options.text: Increase the current in the coil
Add more turns of wire to the coil
Put a soft iron core inside the coil
Reverse the direction of the current
options.feedback: This swaps the poles but does not change the strength.

options.text: Replace the iron core with a plastic rod

practiceQuestions.text: A student finds that an electromagnet with 50 turns and a current of 1.0 A lifts 8 paper clips. The number of clips lifted is roughly proportional to the current. Estimate how many clips the same electromagnet would lift with a current of 2.5 A.
practiceQuestions.hint: The current has increased by a factor of 2.5, so multiply the number of clips by 2.5.

practiceQuestions.text:
A relay is a switch operated by an electromagnet. A small current in the electromagnet coil pulls a soft iron arm, which closes a second circuit carrying a large current to a motor.

(a) Explain why the iron arm is pulled towards the electromagnet when the coil current is switched on. (2 marks)

(b) Explain why the arm is released when the current in the coil is switched off. (1 mark)

(c) Suggest one advantage of using a relay rather than a simple switch to control the motor. (1 mark)
practiceQuestions.hint: For (a), think about induced magnetism and which pole forms on the arm. For (c), consider the safety of the person operating the switch.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) The current in the coil creates a magnetic field; the soft iron arm becomes an induced magnet with the opposite pole nearest the electromagnet, so it is attracted. (b) With no current there is no field, the soft iron loses its magnetism and the arm springs back. (c) The operator only handles the small, safe current; the large current circuit is kept separate, or the motor can be switched remotely.

markScheme.criterion: Current in the coil produces a magnetic field
The iron arm becomes an induced magnet / opposite pole induced so it is attracted
No current means no field so the soft iron loses its magnetism and the arm is released
Operator is isolated from the large current / safer / can control remotely

practiceQuestions.text: A grey metal bar attracts steel paper clips at both ends and is attracted to the north pole of a known magnet. Which further observation would PROVE that the bar is itself a permanent magnet?
practiceQuestions.hint: Both a permanent magnet and a piece of iron can attract things. Only one of them can do the opposite.
practiceQuestions.explanation: An unmagnetised iron bar becomes an induced magnet near any pole and is always attracted, so attraction proves nothing. Repulsion can only happen between two permanent magnets, so if one end of the bar pushes the north pole of the known magnet away, the bar must be a magnet.

options.text: One end of the bar repels the north pole of the known magnet
Both ends of the bar pick up iron filings
options.feedback: An iron bar sitting near a magnet would also do this because it becomes an induced magnet.

options.text: The bar is attracted to the south pole of the known magnet
options.feedback: A plain iron bar is attracted to either pole of a magnet.

options.text: A compass needle turns towards the bar
options.feedback: The compass needle is itself a magnet, so it would induce magnetism in an iron bar and be attracted to it.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: when a steel paper clip hangs from the north pole of a bar magnet, the end of the clip touching the magnet has become a south pole.
practiceQuestions.hint: The clip is an induced magnet. Which pole must face the magnet for the clip to be held on?
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. The magnet induces magnetism in the clip so that the pole nearest to it is the opposite pole. Next to the magnet's north pole the clip gains a south pole, and the unlike poles attract, holding the clip up.

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text: A student draws the magnetic field around a bar magnet. Which THREE statements about the field lines on her diagram are correct?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about which way a plotting compass points, how spacing shows strength, and whether lines can ever meet.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A plotting compass needle lines up along the field line it sits on, pointing the way the line goes. The lines are closest together at the poles, where the field is strongest, and spread out where it is weaker. Field lines never cross, because the field at any point can only have one direction; where two fields overlap they combine into a single new pattern.

options.text: A plotting compass placed on a field line points along the line
The lines are furthest apart where the field is weakest
Outside the magnet, the lines leave the north pole and arrive at the south pole
Field lines cross each other where the fields of two magnets overlap
options.feedback: Field lines never cross; the field at any point has only one direction.

practiceQuestions.text: A student builds an electromagnet from a coil of wire, a battery and an iron nail. Match each change she makes to its effect on the electromagnet.
practiceQuestions.hint: Strength depends on current, number of turns and the core; the direction of the current decides which end is north.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Winding more turns on the coil makes the field stronger. Swapping the battery connections reverses the current, so the north and south poles swap ends without changing the strength. Adding a resistor reduces the current, which makes the field weaker.

pairs.left: Winding extra turns of wire onto the nail
Swapping the two battery connections round
pairs.right: The north and south poles swap ends

pairs.left: Adding a resistor in series to reduce the current

practiceQuestions.text: A long straight wire passes through a horizontal sheet of card. The current in the wire flows directly away from you, into the card. Looking down at the card, which pattern do the magnetic field lines make?
practiceQuestions.hint: Use the right-hand grip rule: point your right thumb away from you and see which way your fingers curl.
practiceQuestions.explanation: With the thumb of the right hand pointing away from the viewer (in the direction of the current), the fingers curl clockwise. The field lines are therefore concentric clockwise circles centred on the wire.

options.text: Clockwise circles centred on the wire
Anticlockwise circles centred on the wire
options.feedback: Anticlockwise would be the pattern for a current coming towards you.

options.text: Straight lines radiating outwards from the wire
Straight lines running parallel to the wire

practiceQuestions.text: A scrapyard crane lifts old cars with an electromagnet whose core is made of soft iron rather than steel. Explain why soft iron is the better choice.
practiceQuestions.hint: The crane operator has to be able to drop the car exactly where it is wanted by switching the current off.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Soft iron is easily magnetised, so when the current flows the core gives a strong magnetic field that can lift the car. When the current is switched off soft iron loses its magnetism immediately, so the car is released. A steel core would stay magnetised as a permanent magnet and the car would remain stuck to it.

markScheme.criterion: Soft iron is easily magnetised / gives a strong field when the current flows
Soft iron loses its magnetism when the current is switched off, whereas steel would stay magnetised

practiceQuestions.text:
A student investigates the magnetic field around a bar magnet using iron filings.

(a) Describe how the student could use the iron filings to show the shape of the magnetic field. (2 marks)

(b) Explain how the pattern shows where the field is strongest, and state what a plotting compass can show that the iron filings cannot. (2 marks)

(c) The student then holds a steel nail near the south pole of the magnet. Explain why the nail is attracted. (1 mark)
practiceQuestions.hint: For (a), think about what has to be placed over the magnet and what the student does to make the filings settle into a pattern. For (b), remember that filings have no arrows.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Place a sheet of card or paper over the magnet, sprinkle iron filings thinly across it and tap the card gently so the filings line up along the field lines. (b) The filings are most crowded together at the poles, and the field is strongest where the lines are closest together. The filings do not show the direction of the field; a plotting compass points from north to south along the line. (c) The nail becomes an induced magnet with a north pole nearest the magnet's south pole, and unlike poles attract.

markScheme.criterion: Place card / paper over the magnet and sprinkle iron filings on it
Tap the card so the filings line up along the field lines
Field is strongest where the filings / lines are closest together, at the poles
Filings do not show the direction of the field; a compass points along the line from north to south
Nail becomes an induced magnet with a north pole nearest the south pole, so unlike poles attract
